tldr: We proposed a control method that geometrically estimates contact locations and normals across the entire hand in real time using a tracked 3D object model and joint angles—without requiring tactile sensors—and optimally redistributes grasp forces as contact states evolve. Real-world experiments demonstrated that the whole hand can adapt and recover from external disturbances, object shifts, and even grasp loss.
hero_caption: Snapshots of approaching, grasping, maintaining, and recovering on a real 27-DoF robot system (Flexiv Rizon 4 and Robotis 5F hand). Even when a human hits or tries to snatch a Pringles can or a box, the system withstands disturbances by redistributing forces across the whole hand, and if dropped, it immediately transitions to reactive reaching to regrasp the object.
overview:
When dexterously grasping an object with a multi-fingered robot hand, simply executing preplanned contact forces or finger configurations often leads to failure. As fingers close, the object moves, or as arm acceleration and external disturbances occur, actual contact locations and surface normals deviate moment by moment from the original plan. Conventional reactive grasping mostly relies on mounting tactile sensors on fingertips to locally adjust forces. However, adapting to contact changes across the "whole hand"—including finger sides, proximal links, and the palm—remains extremely difficult.

To address this, the authors asked: why not solve contacts geometrically from the hand's kinematics and the tracked object's position if tactile sensors are unavailable? By querying the object's signed distance field (SDF) using the robot's joint angles, contact locations and normals across all hand links are estimated in under a millisecond. Then, under dynamically evolving contacts, a quadratic program (QP) is solved in real time to redistribute forces across all links while satisfying friction cone constraints, actuator torque limits, and eliminating unactuated force components that joints cannot generate.

Evaluations in simulation and on a physical system (a 7-DoF arm with a 20-DoF multi-fingered hand) showed substantially higher disturbance resistance compared to baselines that maintain fixed force allocations. Furthermore, by integrating this controller with reactive reaching, the system autonomously maintains and recovers grasps even when subjected to severe human disturbances or when the object is temporarily pulled out of the hand.
contributions: Proposed a method to geometrically estimate contact points and normals across the entire hand in real time without tactile sensors, using hand proprioception (joint angles), object pose tracking, and a 3D object model.

Formulated a robust real-time force allocation QP by introducing an "actuation-consistency constraint" motivated by whole-limb force analysis, suppressing unactuated force components that joint torques cannot produce.

Integrated force regulation with reactive reaching and replanning, demonstrating grasp maintenance under disturbances and autonomous recovery after grasp loss during dynamically changing whole-hand power grasps on real hardware.

sections.heading: The essence of dexterous grasping is tracking contact evolution, not static pose generation
sections.summary: Dexterous multi-fingered grasping cannot succeed merely by reproducing a planned posture; it requires continuously maintaining stability as contacts dynamically shift. This work presents the first hardware system that sequentially estimates whole-hand contacts via hand geometry without tactile sensors and redistributes forces in real time.
sections.details:
Research in dexterous grasping has traditionally focused heavily on how to generate stable grasp postures. However, no matter how perfect the precomputed grasp posture is, the object easily moves inside the hand as fingers close against it, or due to arm motion inertia and external disturbances.

When the object moves, contact positions and normals change. This fundamentally invalidates the grasp matrix (which maps contact forces to the resultant wrench on the object) and the contact Jacobian (which maps contact forces to joint torques). In short, attempting to maintain a contact force distribution computed only once beforehand will inevitably fail.

An ideal grasp effectively utilizes "whole-hand" contacts, including the sides of the fingers, proximal phalanges, and the palm, not just the fingertips. However, covering the entire hand with tactile skins remains difficult due to wiring and durability challenges. Conversely, inverse contact estimation from joint torque residuals becomes underdetermined when multiple contacts occur simultaneously.

This work turns the problem around by "treating the hand itself as a geometric contact sensor." Based on tracked object pose and hand forward kinematics, it geometrically determines which links across the hand are touching the object, directly updating the contact set inside the control loop. This achieves a controller that continuously redistributes forces as contacts appear, break, and slide, all without using any tactile sensors.

sections.heading: A history of contact estimation and force allocation: Shifting from tactile reliance to geometry
sections.summary: Prior work is reviewed across grasp posture generation, contact state estimation, and grasp force allocation. This research overcomes the physical limitations of tactile sensor placement by integrating whole-limb contact mechanics and geometric contact estimation directly into a real-time control loop.
sections.details:
To contextualize this research, let us review three related areas.

### II-A Dexterous Grasp Posture Generation
Techniques for grasp posture generation have advanced significantly, from optimizing force-closure (the ability to resist external forces) to recent generative models trained on large-scale datasets. However, many generated grasps are executed open-loop. They rely on fixed open-loop forces or penetration heuristics after contact, making them fragile to shifts in the contact state.

### II-B Contact State Estimation
Controlling whole-hand forces requires the positions and normal vectors of all contact points. While tactile arrays have been extended toward the palm, wrapping an entire high-DoF multi-fingered hand remains difficult due to wiring and durability issues. Estimating contacts from joint torques works well for single contacts, but becomes indeterminate in whole-hand power grasps with numerous simultaneous contacts. Meanwhile, computer graphics literature routinely calculates contacts geometrically from distances between 3D object models and human hands. Because robots have highly accurate joint proprioception, whole-hand contacts can be reconstructed geometrically with high fidelity as long as the object pose is tracked.

### II-C Grasp Force Allocation Control
Optimally distributing contact forces under friction cone and actuator limits is a classical problem. Recent methods (such as CoorGrasp) formulate online force allocation for arbitrary numbers of contacts, but assume tactile sensors exist at those contact points. This paper crucially differs by substituting tactile sensors with "object geometric models and pose tracking," enabling real-time control of whole-hand contacts including sensorless areas like the palm and finger sides.

sections.heading: Sensing the whole hand without tactile sensors: Geometric estimation and actuation-consistent QP
sections.summary: By querying signed distance fields (SDF) of the object on a GPU, whole-hand contact points and normals are rapidly estimated, and contact forces are recomputed in real time via quadratic programming (QP). It incorporates an actuation-consistency constraint to suppress unactuated forces, seamlessly integrated with reactive reaching.
sections.details:
The complete architecture rests on three pillars: "geometric contact estimation," "real-time force allocation QP," and "integration with reactive reaching."

### III-A & III-B Geometric Contact Estimation
Contact detection is formulated as a geometric query rather than physical sensing. A signed distance field (SDF) is precomputed from the object mesh. About 3,000 candidate points are uniformly sampled across all hand link surfaces. Using current joint angles $q$ and the tracked 6-DoF object pose, these candidate points are transformed into the object frame. By batch-querying the SDF on a GPU via NVIDIA Warp, distance evaluations for all links finish in under 1 ms. Candidate points within a threshold $d_{\mathrm{thresh}}$ (1 cm in experiments) are treated as contacts. For each link, up to $K$ points (5 points in experiments) closest to the surface are retained to form the current contact set $\mathcal{C}_t$.

### III-C Real-Time Grasp Force Allocation and Constraints
For the resulting contact set, a convex quadratic program (QP) is solved at every control cycle to minimize the residual wrench (net force and torque imbalance) on the object. The objective minimizes the norm of the residual wrench $w_c = G f_c$, subject to the following constraints:
- Friction cone constraint: To prevent slip, forces at each contact point are bounded within a linearized four-sided pyramid inscribed inside the Coulomb friction cone.
- Minimum grasp force constraint: To avoid the trivial solution of zero force, the sum of normal forces is constrained to be at least $f_{n,\min}$ (10 N), ensuring a firm squeeze.
- Torque limits: Contact forces on actuated links $f_{\mathrm{act}}$ map to joint torques $\tau_q$ via the transpose of the contact Jacobian $J_{\mathrm{act}}^T$. These torques are bounded by actuator limits $\tau_{\max}$. Unactuated contacts (such as the palm) act as passive reaction forces against external loads.
- Actuation-consistency constraint: This is a core theoretical insight. Force components lying in the null space of the transpose of the contact Jacobian, $\mathrm{Null}(J_{\mathrm{act}}^T)$, cannot be produced by any commanded joint torques. By computing the null space basis $N_u$ via singular value decomposition (SVD), the constraint $\lVert N_u^T f_{\mathrm{act}} \rVert_\infty \leq \epsilon_{\mathrm{margin}}$ (0.5 N) prevents the optimization from relying on uncontrollable forces.

### III-D Integration with Reactive Reaching
To automate behavior before and after reaching a grasp, reactive reaching from prior work is extended and integrated. Fingertip and palm poses are tracked via a joint-velocity QP, continuously following the object even if it moves. When geometric conditions are met (the thumb and at least two other fingers establish contact), control hands off to force regulation. Conversely, if the object exits the convex hull of the fingers and palm, it is treated as a grasp loss, triggering an automatic return to reactive reaching via a finite state machine.

captions.F2: Perturbation test protocol used in simulation. (a, b) After grasp initialization, force control starts; (c) a load equal to 10% of the object weight is sequentially applied along 6 orthogonal directions to test retention. (d) The object is rotated about a random axis using a virtual spring-damper to induce slippage, and (e) the 6-directional load is applied again to evaluate whether the grasp is maintained.

sections.heading: Re-securing slipping objects: Validation in simulation and on hardware
sections.summary: In simulation across 79 YCB objects, grasp retention under dynamic perturbations improved significantly over baselines, and ablations validated the actuation-consistency constraint and choice of contact count. Hardware experiments also demonstrated strong retention and recovery against severe human disturbances and snatches.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Evaluation
Evaluations were conducted in the MuJoCo physics engine across 79 objects and 790 power grasps from the YCB dataset. Gravity was disabled to assess pure grasping capability, and load tests were performed by applying forces equal to 10% of object weight along 6 directions ($\pm x, \pm y, \pm z$).
- Robustness to dynamic perturbations: When objects were forcibly rotated from 0° to 90°, feedforward control (retaining initial contact forces) and task-space impedance control suffered severe performance drops. In contrast, the proposed method retained an 88.6% grasp success rate even under 90° rotational disturbances. Furthermore, running the proposed method on fingertip links alone achieved only 72.4%, highlighting the necessity of utilizing links across the entire hand.
- Initial contact count and stability: Grasps with fewer initial contacts (3–5 points) caused baselines to fail frequently (32–56% success) due to slight object shifts during initial finger closure. The proposed method maintained an 82–95% success rate by immediately updating contacts and forces as the object shifted.

### IV-B Ablation Studies
- Effect of the actuation-consistency constraint: As shown in Figure F5, omitting this constraint caused the QP to seek solutions requiring forces the joints could not produce, leaving a residual net force of 0.428 N at the object center of mass. Enforcing the constraint reduced the actual net force to nearly zero.
- Robustness to object pose error: When artificial tracking biases up to 30° and 5 mm were injected, baseline success dropped to 54%, whereas the proposed method maintained 87–93% success (peaking at 93% with $d_{\mathrm{thresh}}=1$ cm).
- Contact points per link $K$: Comparing $K=1$ through $K=7$ showed that $K=5$ yielded the highest success rate (93.2%). While more points capture contact patches more accurately, they increase QP solve times and drop the control frequency from 227 Hz down to 66 Hz, demonstrating a trade-off between speed and geometric expressiveness.

### IV-C Real-World Experiments
Experiments used a 27-DoF setup: a 7-DoF Flexiv Rizon 4 arm, a 20-DoF Robotis 5F hand, and a RealSense D455 RGB-D camera. Objects were pre-scanned using 2D Gaussian Splatting, and a FoundationPose-based tracker provided 6-DoF poses at 30 Hz.
- Human disturbances and autonomous recovery: A total of 78 disturbance trials were conducted on Pringles cans and boxes, including poking and twisting with a stick, moving the object mid-reach, and snatching it away after grasp. Grasp loss occurred only 8 times; in 6 of those trials, the object stayed in the workspace, allowing the controller to return to reactive reaching and regrasp without human intervention.
- Exploiting dorsal (back-of-finger) contacts: As shown in Figure F10, even in an unconventional interleaved grasp where the object was pinched by the dorsal sides of the fingers, geometric estimation accurately identified the contact on the back of the pinky finger and allocated forces, successfully retaining the object against disturbances.

captions.F5: Comparison of contact forces with and without the actuation-consistency constraint. Blue shows desired force, green shows measured force, and red shows the measured resultant wrench at the object's center of mass. Without the constraint (left), the solver requests forces the joints cannot generate, causing a large residual force (red arrow). With the constraint (right), the measured net force is near zero, ensuring stability.
captions.F10: Experiment with an unconventional grasp interleaving the palmar and dorsal (back) sides of the fingers. Geometric estimation accurately detects the contact and its motion on the dorsal side of the little finger (cyan circle), showing stable force allocation and retention even on atypical contact surfaces.

sections.heading: Summary and future work: Strengths and limits of the geometric approach
sections.summary: A real-time whole-hand force regulation framework using only geometry and joint angles without tactile sensors has been established. The authors also identify practical challenges, such as tracking failure under severe occlusion, normal vector flipping on thin objects, and the absence of dynamic external force compensation under quasi-static assumptions.
sections.details:
This work demonstrated on physical hardware that whole-hand adaptive force regulation is achievable without covering the body in tactile sensors, by directly linking object shape and pose tracking with robot geometry inside the control loop. Its flexibility—treating contacts on all links equally, including the back of fingers, without relying on grasp taxonomies or tactile sensor layouts—is particularly compelling.

At the same time, the authors acknowledge clear limitations:
- Heavy dependence on pose tracking: If the hand severely occludes the object and blocks the camera view, tracking fails and contact estimation collapses.
- Vulnerability to thin objects: For objects only a few millimeters thick, slight tracking errors can misplace hand surface points onto the opposite side of the object, flipping calculated contact normals by 180 degrees.
- Quasi-static assumptions: The framework resists disturbances through friction via squeezing rather than explicitly estimating and compensating for gravity, inertia, or external wrenches, limiting performance under rapid dynamic accelerations.
- Unmodeled passive compliance: While the actuation-consistency constraint conservatively excludes forces that joint torques cannot generate, it does not model real-world compliance or passive preloading at the contact interface.

Future directions include improving robustness when visual tracking degrades and extending the controller to account for contact compliance and full system dynamics.

takeaways: Overturns the assumption that links without tactile sensors cannot be used for force control: querying SDFs against 3D models and tracked poses turns the whole hand into a millisecond-fast geometric contact sensor.

Using SVD to enforce an "actuation-consistency constraint" from whole-limb mechanics effectively removes unactuated force components (the null space of the contact Jacobian transpose) from the QP, preventing unwanted residual forces on hardware.

Adapting to contact changes across the entire hand—including proximal links and the palm—yields significantly higher grasp retention under disturbances than adapting fingertips alone (88.6% vs 72.4% under 90° rotational perturbation).

Structuring reaching, force regulation, and regrasp triggers via geometric state transitions creates an autonomous recovery mechanism that seamlessly retrieves dropped objects without complex planning.
limitations: Requires an accurate 3D mesh and uninterrupted 6-DoF object pose tracking, making it vulnerable to failure under severe visual occlusion by the hand.
Prone to failure on thin objects (a few millimeters thick), where small tracking inaccuracies can cause contact normals to flip 180 degrees.

Relies on a quasi-static approach that resists disturbances through frictional squeezing rather than explicitly estimating and canceling gravity, inertia, or external forces, limiting its effectiveness in high-speed dynamic manipulation.
